Abstract

1 Proteins move and deform to ensure their biological functions. Despite significant   
2 progress in protein structure prediction, approximating conformational ensembles at   
3 physiological conditions remains a fundamental open problem. This paper presents   
4 a novel perspective on the problem by directly targeting continuous compact rep  
5 resentations of protein motions inferred from sparse experimental observations.   
6 We develop a task-specific loss function enforcing data symmetries, including   
7 scaling and permutation operations. Our method PETIMOT (Protein sEquence and   
8 sTructure-based Inference of MOTions) leverages transfer learning from pre-trained   
9 protein language models through an SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network. When   
10 trained and evaluated on the Protein Data Bank, PETIMOT shows superior perfor  
11 mance in time and accuracy, capturing protein dynamics, particularly large/slow   
12 conformational changes, compared to state-of-the-art flow-matching approaches   
13 and traditional physics-based models. Our code and protocols are available at   
14 https: // anonymous. 4open. science/ r/ PETIMOT-4ED4/ .
15 1 Introduction

16 Proteins orchestrate biological processes in living organisms by interacting with their environment   
17 and adapting their three-dimensional (3D) structures to engage with cellular partners, including   
18 other proteins, nucleic acids, small-molecule ligands, and co-factors. In recent years, spectacular   
19 advances in high-throughput deep learning (DL) technologies have provided access to reliable   
20 predictions of protein 3D structures at the scale of entire proteomes [1]. These breakthroughs have   
21 also highlighted the complexities of protein conformational heterogeneity. State-of-the-art predictors   
22 struggle to model alternative conformations, fold switches, large-amplitude conformational changes,   
23 and solution ensembles [2].   
24 The success of AlphaFold2 [3] has stimulated machine-learning approaches focused on inference  
25 time interventions in the model to generate structural diversity. They include enabling or increasing   
26 dropout [4, 5], or manipulating the evolutionary information given as input to the model [6–9].   
27 Despite promising results on specific families, several studies have emphasised the difficulties in   
28 rationalising the effectiveness of these modifications and interpreting them [10, 11]. Moreover,   
29 these cannot be transferred to protein language model-based predictors that do not rely on multiple   
30 sequence alignments. Researchers have also actively engaged in the development of deep-learning   
31 frameworks based on diffusion, or the more general flow matching, to generate conformational   
32 ensembles [12]. While family-specific models proved useful in exploring native-like conformational   
33 landscapes, models trained across protein families still fail to approximate solution ensembles [13].   
34 This work presents a new glance at the protein conformational diversity problem. Instead of learning   
35 and sampling from multi-dimensional empirical distributions, we propose to learn eigenspaces (the   
36 structure) of the positional covariance matrices in collections of experimental 3D structures and   
37 generalize these over different homology levels. Our motivation is that the diversity present within   
38 different 3D structures of the same protein or close homologs is a good proxy for the conformational   
39 heterogeneity of proteins in solution [14] and can generally be (almost fully) explained by a small set   
40 of linear vectors, also referred to as modes [15, 16]. Although linear spaces may not be well-suited   
41 for capturing highly complex non-linear motions, such as loop deformations, they offer multiple   
42 advantages. These include faster learning due to the reduced complexity of the model, improved   
43 explainability as the components directly correspond to interpretable data dimensions, faster inference,   
44 and the straightforward combination or integration of multiple data dimensions.

45 To summarize, our main contributions are:

• We provide a novel formulation of the protein conformational diversity problem.   
• We present a novel benchmark representative of the Protein Data Bank structural diversity and compiled with a robust pipeline [15], along with data- and task-specific metrics.   
• We develop a SE(3)-equivariant Graph Neural Network architecture equipped with a novel symmetry-aware loss function for comparing linear subspaces, with invariance to permutation and scaling. Our model, PETIMOT, leverages embeddings from pre-trained protein language models (pLMs), building on prior proof-of-concept work demonstrating that they encode information about functional protein motions [17].   
• PETIMOT is trained on sparse experimental data without any use of simulation data, in contrast with Timewarp for instance [18]. Moreover, our model does not require physicsbased guidance or feedback, unlike [12] for instance.   
• Our results demonstrate the capability of PETIMOT to generalise across protein families (contrary to variational autoencoder-based approaches) and to compare favorably in running time and accuracy to AlphaFlow, ESMFlow, and the Normal Mode Analysis.
60 2 Related Works

61 Protein structure prediction. AlphaFold2 was the first end-to-end deep neural network to achieve   
62 near-experimental accuracy in predicting protein 3D structures, even for challenging cases with   
63 low sequence similarity to proteins with resolved structures [3]. It extracts information from an   
64 input multiple sequence alignment (MSA) and outputs all-atom 3D coordinates. Later works have   
65 shown that substituting the input alignment by embeddings from a protein language model can yield   
66 comparable performance [19–22].   
67 Generating conformational ensembles. Beyond the single-structure frontier, several studies have   
68 underscored the limitations and potential of protein structure predictors (PSP) for generating al  
69 ternative conformations [23, 24, 11, 2]. Approaches focused on re-purposing AlphaFold2 include   
70 dropout-based massive sampling [4, 5], guiding the predictions with state-annotated templates   
71 [25, 26], and inputting shallow, masked, corrupted, subsampled or clustered alignments [6–9]. De  
72 spite promising results, these approaches remain computationally expensive and their generalisability,   
73 interpretability, and controllability remain unclear [11, 2]. More recent works have aimed at overcom  
74 ing these limitations by directly optimising PSP learnt embeddings under low-dimensional ensemble   
75 constraints [27].   
76 Another line of research has consisted in fine-tuning or re-training AlphaFold2 and other single  
77 state PSP under diffusion or flow matching frameworks [28, 13, 29]. For instance, the Al  
78 phaFlow/ESMFlow method progressively denoises samples drawn from a harmonic prior under   
79 flow field controlled by AlphaFold or ESMFold [28]. It compares favourably with MSA subsam  
80 pling or clustering baselines, with a substantially superior precision-diversity Pareto frontier. More   
81 generally, diffusion- and flow matching-based models allow for efficiently generating diverse confor  
82 mations conditioned on the presence of ligands or cellular partners [30, 31, 12, 32, 33]. Despite their   
83 strengths, these techniques are prone to hallucination.   
84 Parallel related works have sought to directly learn generative models of equilibrium Boltzmann   
85 distributions using normalising flows [34, 18], or machine-learning force fields based on equivariant   
86 graph neural network (GNN) representations [35], to enhance or replace molecular dynamics (MD)   
87 simulations.   
88 Protein conformational heterogeneity manifold learning. Unsupervised, physics-based Normal   
89 Mode Analysis (NMA) has long been effective for inferring functional modes of deformation by   
90 leveraging the topology of a single protein 3D structure [36–38]. While appealing for its compu  
91 tational efficiency, the accuracy of NMA strongly depends on the initial topology [39], limiting   
92 its ability to model extensive secondary structure rearrangements. Recent efforts have sought to   
93 address these limitations by directly learning continuous, compact representations of protein motions   
94 from sparse experimental 3D structures. These approaches employ dimensionality reduction tech  
95 niques, from classical manifold learning methods [15] to neural network architectures like variational   
96 auto-encoders [40]. By projecting motions onto a learned low-dimensional manifold, these meth  
97 ods enable reconstruction of accurate, physico-chemically realistic conformations, both within the   
98 interpolation regime and near the convex hull of the training data [15]. Additionally, they assist in   
99 identifying collective variables from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, supporting importance  
100 sampling strategies [41–45]. Despite these advances, such approaches are currently constrained to   
101 family-specific models.   
102 E(3)-equivariant graph neural networks. Graph Neural Networks (GNN) have been extensively   
103 used to represent protein 3D structures. They are robust to transformations of the Euclidean group,   
104 namely rotations, reflections, and translations, as well as to permutations. In their simplest formulation,   
105 each node represents an atom and any pair of atoms are connected by an edge if their distance is   
106 smaller than a cutoff or among the smallest $k$ interatomic distances. Many works have proposed   
107 to enrich this graph representation with SE(3)-equivariant features informing the model about   
108 interatomic directions and orientations [46–49, 31, 50]. For instance, VisNet captures the full local   
109 geometric information, including bonds, angles, as well as dihedral torsion and improper angles with   
110 node-wise high-order geometric tensors [50]. Moreover, to go beyond local 3D neighbourhoods while   
111 maintaining sub-quadratic complexity, Chroma adds in randomly sampled long-range connections   
112 [31].

180 Dual-Track Representation. PETIMOT processes protein sequences through a message-passing   
181 neural network that simultaneously handles residue embeddings and motion vectors in local coordinate   
182 frames (Fig. 1). For each residue $i$ , we define and update a node embedding $\mathbf { s } _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { d }$ initialized   
183 from protein language model features and a set of $K$ motion vectors $\{ \vec { x } _ { i k } \} _ { k = 1 } ^ { K } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { 3 \times K }$ initialized   
184 randomly. The message passing procedure is detailed in Algorithm B.1 of Appendix B.2.   
185 Graph Construction. The protein is represented as a graph where nodes correspond to the residues,   
186 and edges capture spatial relationships. For each residue $i$ , we connect to its $k$ nearest neighbors based   
187 on $\mathbf { \boldsymbol { C } } \alpha$ distances and $l$ randomly selected residues. This hybrid connectivity scheme ensures both local   
188 geometric consistency and global information flow, while maintaining sparsity for computational   
189 efficiency. Indeed, our model scales linearly with the length $N$ of a protein. In our base model we set   
190 $k = 5$ and $l = 1 0$ .   
191 Node features. We chose ProstT5 as our default protein language model for initialising node   
192 embeddings [57]. This structure-aware pLM offers an excellent balance between model size –   
193 including the number of parameters and embedding dimensionality – and performance [17].   
194 Local Reference Frames. Each residue’s backbone atoms (N, CA, C) define a local reference frame   
195 through a rigid transformation $T _ { i } \in S E ( 3 )$ . For each residue pair $( i , j )$ , we compute their relative   
196 transformation $T _ { i j } = T _ { i } ^ { - 1 } \circ T _ { j }$ from which we extract the rotation $R _ { i j } \in S O ( 3 )$ and translation   
197 $\vec { t } _ { i j } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { 3 }$ . Under global rotations and translations of the protein, these relative transformations remain   
198 invariant.   
199 Edge Features. Edge features $e _ { i j }$ provide an SE(3)-invariant encoding of the protein structure   
200 through relative orientations, translational offsets, protein chain distance, and a complete description   
201 of peptide plane positioning captured by pairwise backbone atom distances. See Appendix B.3 for   
202 more details. The training procedure is detailed in Appendix B.4.

text: Contribution of sequence and structure features. We performed an ablation study to assess the contribution of sequence and structure information to our architecture. Our results show that ProstT5 slightly outperforms the more recent and larger pLM, ESM-Cambrian 600M [58] (Fig. B.2). Geometrical information about protein structure provides the most significant contribution, as replacing ProstT5 embeddings with random numbers has only a small impact on network performance. Conversely, the network’s performance without structural information strongly depends on the chosen pLM. While the structure-aware embeddings from ProstT5 partially compensate for missing 3D structure information, relying solely on ESM-C embeddings results in poor performance (Fig. B.2). Moreover, connecting each residue to its 15 nearest neighbours (sorted according to $\mathbf { C } \alpha \cdot$ -Cα distances) in the protein graph results in lower performance compared to introducing randomly chosen edges or even fully relying on random connectivity (Fig. B.4).

252 Generalisation capability. Because our conformational collections are defined based on $80 \%$   
253 sequence identity and coverage thresholds, some test proteins may be close homologs of the training   
254 proteins. Yet, the sequence identity and structural similarity (TM-score) of the test proteins with   
255 respect to the training set do not determine the quality of PETIMOT predictions (Fig. C.3). PETIMOT   
256 provides high-quality predictions for a number of test proteins that do not share any detectable   
257 similarity and only weak structural similarity (TM-score below 0.5) to the training set. To further   
258 assess PETIMOT’s generalisation capability across protein families, we implemented a more stringent   
259 train-validation-test split using a $30 \%$ sequence similarity threshold. This process involved three key   
260 steps: (1) removing from training and validation sets any proteins sharing ${ > } 3 0 \%$ sequence similarity   
261 with test proteins, (2) redefining these sets through random splitting at the $30 \%$ sequence identity level,   
262 and (3) reducing redundancy within each set to ensure balanced representation of protein families   
263 (detailed in Appendix B.6). When trained under this stringent protocol, PETIMOT achieved a success   
264 rate of $4 0 . 8 7 \%$ on our non-redundant set of 734 test proteins, consistently outperforming all baseline   
265 methods (see Appendix Fig. C.4a-b). This demonstrates our architecture’s robustness, as the more   
266 challenging similarity restrictions did not dramatically reduce performance. For direct comparison   
267 between our two model versions PETIMOT-default (trained with $80 \%$ similarity threshold) and   
268 PETIMOT-stringent (trained with $30 \%$ non-redundant threshold) we evaluated performance on 474   
269 test proteins that share less than $30 \%$ sequence similarity with any protein used in training or   
270 validation of either model. PETIMOT-stringent achieved a slightly higher success rate $( 4 3 . 6 7 \% )$   
271 compared to PETIMOT-default $( 4 1 . 9 8 \% )$ (see Appendix Fig. C.4c-d). This result emphasizes the   
272 benefit of encouraging better generalization to evolutionary distant protein families through enhanced   
273 data splitting strategies.

Limitations. One current limitation of our approach is the scarcity of functional motions in the training set, raising concerns about its accuracy and completeness. The success rates computed for PETIMOT, although higher than the baseline methods, remain modest, suggesting that some ground-truth motions may lack biological or physical relevance. They may result from experimental artifacts, most often of crystallographic origin. Nevertheless, establishing objective criteria to reliably distinguish artifactual conformations from biologically relevant ones remains infeasible. Our working assumption is that a subset of the conformational manifold in a protein collection always represents functional motions. To address this challenge, we designed our training loss function specifically to evaluate submanifolds by calculating the minimum error between each reference motion and the set of predicted motions, allowing the model to capture conformational diversity while mitigating the impact of potential artefacts.

293 Another limitation is that we do not account for the different time scales at which different types of   
294 protein motions occur. We do not have this temporal information in the PDB training set. The only   
295 information we have is the proxy of the amplitudes of the motions, represented by the eigenvalues in   
296 the original collections. However, these amplitudes might not be relevant as they strongly depend   
297 on the uneven sampling in the PDB and different experimental conditions and temperatures. This   
298 motivated us to only reconstruct the shape of the motion manifolds, not their amplitudes or effective   
299 timescales.   
300 In addition, our approach is limited to modeling protein motions as linear displacement vectors.   
301 While this approximation is sufficient to describe most of the observed conformational heterogeneity,   
302 it remains inadequate for modeling highly complex non-linear deformations. Furthermore, deforming   
303 proteins structures along linear motion direction may produce unrealistic conformations at large   
304 amplitudes. A possible solution yet to be investigated would be the nonlinear extrapolation technique   
305 that have been widely used in molecular mechanics [37]. Finally, a direction for future improvement   
306 would be to provide per-residue confidence estimates for the predicted motions.
07 5 Conclusion

In this work, we have proposed a new perspective on the problem of capturing protein continuous conformational heterogeneity. Compared to state-of-the-art methods, our approach goes beyond generating alternative protein conformations by directly inferring compact and continuous representations of protein motions. Our comprehensive analysis of PETIMOT’s predictive capabilities demonstrates its performance and utility for understanding how proteins deform to perform their functions. Our work opens ways to future developments in protein motion manifold learning, with exciting potential applications in protein engineering and drug development.

Broader impacts. This paper presents work aimed at advancing the field of computational biology and machine learning, specifically in the context of understanding protein dynamics. While the goal is primarily to enhance scientific understanding and methodological rigor, there are potential societal consequences to consider. These include the facilitation of drug discovery and protein engineering applications, as well as ethical concerns regarding the dual use of protein modeling. We emphasize the importance of using these tools responsibly to maximize benefits while mitigating risks. Beyond these considerations, there are no specific societal implications we feel require urgent attention.

588 B.3 SE(3)-equivariant features

We represent protein structures as attributed graphs. The node embeddings are computed with the pre-trained protein language model ProstT5 [57]. It is a fine-tuned version of the sequence-only model T5 that translates amino acid sequences into sequences of discrete structural states and reciprocally.

The edge embeddings are computed using SE(3)-invariant features derived from the input backbone, similarly to prior works [31, 48, 46]. Specifically, the features associated with the edge $e _ { i j }$ from node (atom) $i$ to node (atom) $j$ are:

• Quaternion representation: A 4-dimensional quaternion encoding the relative rotation $R _ { i j }$ between the local reference frames of residues $i$ and $j$ .   
• Relative translation: A 3-dimensional vector representing the translation $\vec { t _ { i j } }$ between the local reference frames.   
• Chain separation: The sequence separation between residues $i$ and $j$ , encoded as $\log ( | i -$ $j | { + } 1 )$ .

B.6 Generalisability assessment across protein families

Protein folds are not evenly represented in the PDB, with some folds being significantly more abundant than others. For our default training procedure, we chose not to correct for this bias because the same fold may exhibit different motions in different collections. This represents a fundamental difference from structure prediction tasks, where distant homologs often exhibit nearly identical 3D structures. In contrast, for protein motion prediction, even proteins with the same fold can display dramatically different conformational changes depending on their specific biological context, binding partners, or experimental conditions. Furthermore, the diversity of motions within a single fold family provides valuable information for our model to learn the relationship between sequence, structure, and dynamic behavior.

664 Nevertheless, to rigorously assess PETIMOT’s capability to generalise across protein families, we   
665 re-trained and re-evaluated the model using a more stringent and non-redundant training-validation  
666 test splitting scheme. Specifically, we considered clusters of protein chains defined at $30 \%$ sequence   
667 identity and $80 \%$ sequence coverage using MMseqs2 [62]. These clusters define distant protein   
668 families and we refer to them as clus-30 in the following. We kept the 824 test proteins used for   
669 comparison with other methods as is and we removed all collections belonging to the same clus-30   
670 clusters as these proteins from the training and validation sets. Then, we re-defined a training  
671 validation random split at the level of the clus-30 clusters with a 9:1 ratio. This operation ensures   
672 that any pair of training-validation, training-test or validation-test collections do not share more than   
673 $30 \%$ sequence identity. Finally, for each training or validation clus-30 cluster, we randomly drew 5   
674 samples. This step ensures that each protein family is evenly represented in the training and validation   
675 sets. We also redundancy reduced the test set of 824 proteins (test-824), keeping only one protein for   
676 each clus-30 cluster, which led to 734 proteins (test-734).
